hook.situation: You open a Korean app and see 안녕하세요. You have no idea what any of those shapes mean. Then someone tells you: each block is one spoken syllable, and the shapes literally show you where to put your mouth. You try 한 — it's ㅎ (breath from the throat) + ㅏ (mouth open wide) + ㄴ (tongue behind teeth). Suddenly the writing system makes sense.
objectives: Read any syllable block by identifying its consonant and vowel components
Produce the basic consonants ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ ㅈ ㅎ and basic vowels ㅏ ㅓ ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ ㅣ
Use romanization only as a checking tool, not as a pronunciation crutch
hook.whyItMatters: Every other chapter in this course is built on Hangul. If you skip this and rely on romanization, you will mispronounce Korean for months — romanization uses English spelling habits that do not match Korean sounds. Twenty minutes with Hangul now saves hundreds of hours of re-learning later. King Sejong designed this alphabet to be learned in a single morning, and he was right.

grammarNotes.title: 자음 (Consonants) — Ten Core Shapes
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of consonants as MOUTH BLUEPRINTS. Each shape is a rough sketch of the part of your mouth that makes the sound. ㄱ looks like the back of the throat closing (a bent shape, like the back of your tongue pressing up). ㄴ looks like the tongue tip touching the roof of the mouth. ㅁ is a closed mouth (a box). ㅂ adds lips opening from that box. ㅅ is two lines like teeth. Once you see the blueprint, the sound is no longer random — it is a diagram.
grammarNotes.formation: Consonant placed at the top-left of a syllable block (onset position) or at the bottom (coda position, called 받침)

examples.note: ㄱ makes a 'g/k' sound — the shape curves like the back of the throat closing. Same consonant, different vowels produce different syllables
ㄴ = 'n' — the shape shows the tongue tip pressed to the ridge behind the upper teeth; this is exactly the mouth position for 'n'
ㅁ = 'm' — literally a box representing a closed mouth; lips close for 'm', which is what the box shape shows
ㅂ = 'b/p' — the box (ㅁ) opens at the top as lips part; the two top strokes represent the lips opening

examples.en: ㅇ as a silent placeholder — no consonant sound
examples.note: ㅇ in the onset (top) position is silent — it is a zero-sound placeholder so the syllable block can be built. When ㅇ appears at the bottom (받침), it makes an 'ng' sound

a.en: da — 'd' made with the tongue flat against the ridge

b.en: na — 'n' also made with the tongue at the same ridge

contrastPairs.explanation: ㄷ and ㄴ look similar and use the same part of the mouth. The difference: ㄴ lets air flow through the nose (nasal), while ㄷ blocks and releases air through the mouth (stop). ㄴ has a curved foot shape; ㄷ adds a top horizontal line, making it 'heavier' — visually and phonetically.

Both ㅅ and ㅈ involve the front of the mouth. ㅅ (two lines like teeth) is a light 's/sh' shape. ㅈ adds a horizontal base, increasing the pressure to produce 'j'. More strokes in Hangul often means more mouth pressure for the sound.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: Reading 이 as 'ee' (as in 'see') — exactly like English
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 이 is close to English 'ee' but shorter and unrounded — and only approximately. The real fix is to listen to a native speaker and imitate, not to map to English sounds.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers instinctively reach for their own vowel sounds when they see romanization. But Korean 이 is not English 'ee', Korean 으 has no English equivalent at all, and Korean ㄹ is not 'r' or 'l'. Romanization is a temporary scaffold — use it to check yourself, but learn the actual sounds by ear. The earlier you stop reading romanization as English, the faster your pronunciation improves.

exceptions: ㄹ is romanized as 'r' between vowels (바람 = baram) and as 'l' at the end of a syllable (달 = dal), but it is neither the English 'r' nor 'l' — it is a single Korean sound that you learn by ear
ㅇ is silent at the start of a syllable but pronounced 'ng' at the bottom (받침): 강 = gang, 방 = bang
Some consonants sound different depending on their position in the word — this is called consonant assimilation and you will learn it naturally as your listening improves

grammarNotes.title: 모음 (Vowels) — Lines, Dots, and Direction
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of vowels as a COMPASS ROSE. Every basic Korean vowel is built from three strokes: a vertical line (|), a horizontal line (—), and a short tick that points like a compass needle. The tick's direction tells you the sound. When the tick points RIGHT from a vertical line → ㅏ (open 'a'). When it points LEFT → ㅓ (deeper 'uh'). Tick ABOVE a horizontal line → ㅗ ('o'). Tick BELOW → ㅜ ('oo'). No tick on horizontal → ㅡ (flat 'eu'). Vertical line alone → ㅣ ('ee'). Once you see the compass, you never forget which way the vowel sounds.
grammarNotes.formation: Tall vowels (ㅏ ㅓ ㅣ ㅐ ㅔ) sit to the RIGHT of the consonant. Wide vowels (ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ) sit BELOW the consonant. Combined vowels are built by merging two basic vowels.

examples.en: ㅏ vs ㅓ — both tall vowels beside the consonant
examples.note: ㅏ: tick points RIGHT — mouth open, sound comes forward. ㅓ: tick points LEFT — sound pulls back in the throat. The tick is the only difference on the page and in your mouth.

examples.en: ㅗ vs ㅜ — both wide vowels below the consonant
examples.note: ㅗ: tick points UP from the horizontal line — lips round and rise. ㅜ: tick points DOWN — lips round and drop. The compass direction = the lip movement direction.

examples.en: ㅡ vs ㅣ — no tick needed
examples.note: ㅡ: just the horizontal bar — the mouth is flat and neutral, no rounding. ㅣ: just the vertical bar — teeth close, sound is 'ee'. These are the simplest vowel shapes.
ㅐ (ㅏ+ㅣ) and ㅔ (ㅓ+ㅣ) look similar and in modern Korean are often pronounced identically as a mid-front 'e' sound. Beginners can treat them the same.
ㅗ+ㅏ = ㅘ (wa), ㅜ+ㅓ = ㅝ (wo/weo), ㅜ+ㅣ = ㅟ (wi). These compound vowels are built by stacking two base vowels — you can decode them by recognizing the parts

a.en: bo — tall 'o', lips rounded, sound rises

b.en: bu — deep 'oo', lips rounded, sound drops

contrastPairs.explanation: Same consonant ㅂ, different vowels. ㅗ sits with its tick pointing UP — the vowel shape tells you the sound moves upward/forward in the mouth. ㅜ has its tick pointing DOWN — the sound descends to a deeper 'oo'. The visual and physical direction match.

ㅏ and ㅓ look almost the same but the tick faces opposite directions. ㅏ faces right (toward open space) → mouth opens. ㅓ faces left (inward) → the sound retreats to the back of the mouth. This is not coincidence — King Sejong's design mapped physical articulation to visual direction.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: Pronouncing 으 (ㅡ) as 'oo' or 'u' based on romanization 'eu'
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 으 has no English equivalent — it is a central unrounded vowel. Keep your lips flat (no rounding) and the tongue in the middle of the mouth.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: The romanization 'eu' looks like the French 'eu' or English 'uh', so beginners round their lips. But 으 is made with flat, unrounded lips — the opposite of 'oo'. To train this sound: say 'ee' (이) and keep your lips in exactly that flat position, then move your tongue back. The sound you get is 으. Practice 이 then 으 back and forth.

exceptions: ㅢ (의) is technically ㅡ+ㅣ but in natural speech it often sounds like just 이 (ee) or 에 (e) depending on position: 의사 = 'uisa' (doctor) but the particle 의 usually sounds like 에
Vowel length (long vs. short) existed in classical Korean but modern Seoul Korean has largely lost it — beginners can ignore vowel length completely
Some compound vowels like ㅙ (ㅗ+ㅐ) and ㅞ (ㅜ+ㅔ) are rare and sound very similar to ㅘ and ㅝ respectively

exampleSentence.note: Subject marker 은 attaches to 한글 — you will learn this particle in Chapter 2
이에요 means 'is/am/are' — the simplest Korean copula; perfect for labeling what something is
는 is the topic marker for vowel-ending words — 모음 ends in ㅁ so it uses 은, but ㅏ alone ends in a vowel, so 는 attaches
뭐예요 = 'what is it?' — an essential question frame for asking about unfamiliar characters

exampleSentence.en: What is the sound of this character?
exampleSentence.note: 의 is a possessive particle — '글자의 소리' = 'the sound of the character'
있어요 (there is / to have) — the final ㄴ in 한 is the 받침; not all syllables have one
A natural comment to make as a beginner — acknowledges that pronunciation takes practice
Polite form 읽어요 — the verb stem 읽 + 어요; note the pronunciation shifts from 'ikda' to 'ilgeoyo' due to consonant assimilation
쓰다 is ㅡ-irregular: the ㅡ drops before 아/어, giving 써요 not 쓰어요
듣다 is ㄷ-irregular: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending → 들어요, not 듣어요
말하다 → 말해요 in polite form; 천천히 = slowly — essential classroom vocabulary
따라 하세요 is a polite command — very common in language class settings
One of the most useful phrases for a beginner — you will say this constantly in your first weeks of Korean
다시 comes before the verb it modifies — Korean adverbs do not change form
알겠어요 literally means 'I will know it' (future-inference form of 알다) but functions as 'I get it now' — use it as a fixed phrase

extendedVocabulary.english: I don't know / I'm not sure

exampleSentence.note: The counterpart to 알겠어요 — equally important to have in your first lesson vocabulary
매일 = every day; 연습하다 follows the 하다 verb pattern — 연습 (practice noun) + 하다 (to do)

extendedDialogue.setting: Jiyeon (a Korean tutor) meets Minjun (a complete beginner) for their first online lesson

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 안녕하세요! 저는 지연이에요. 오늘 한글을 공부해요.
lines.romanization: Annyeonghaseyo! Jeoneun jiyeonieyo. Oneul hangeureul gongbuhaeyo.
lines.en: Hello! I'm Jiyeon. Today we study Hangul.
lines.grammarNote: 지연이에요 = 'I am Jiyeon' — the copula 이에요 attaches after a consonant-final name (지연 ends in ㄴ)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Hello. I'm Minjun. Is Hangul difficult?
lines.grammarNote: Rising intonation turns 어려워요 (it's difficult) into a yes/no question — Korean does not need a separate question word for this

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: No, it's easy! Hangul is a sound-based script.
lines.grammarNote: 글자예요 = 'it is a character/script' — 이에요 shortens to 예요 after a vowel-final word (글자 ends in ㅏ vowel)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.grammarNote: 이게 = 이것이 (this thing + subject marker), contracted; 뭐예요 = 'what is it?' — the most useful question for new learners

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.en: It's ㅏ. It's a vowel. The sound is 'a'.
lines.grammarNote: Three short sentences in a row — Korean naturally uses short complete sentences instead of one long sentence with relative clauses

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: I see. Please say it again.
lines.grammarNote: 다시 말해 주세요 = V + 아/어 주세요 (please do for me) — the pattern-015 request form; 말하다 → 말해 + 주세요

lines.speaker: 지연
lines.ko: 좋아요. 천천히 해요. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ — 기본 모음이에요.
lines.romanization: Joayo. Cheoncheonhi haeyo. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ — gibon moeumieyo.
lines.en: Good. Let's go slowly. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ — these are the basic vowels.
lines.grammarNote: 기본 = basic/fundamental; 이에요 after the consonant-final 음 again — this copula pattern will become automatic

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 따라 할게요. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. 맞아요?
lines.romanization: Ttara halgeyo. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. Majayo?
lines.en: I'll repeat after you. ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. Is that right?
lines.grammarNote: 할게요 = 'I will do' (first-person intention); 맞아요? = 'Is that correct?' — essential self-checking question for language learners

readingText.title: 민준의 첫 한글 공부 (Minjun's First Hangul Study)
readingText.body: 오늘 처음으로 한글을 공부했어요. 한글은 자음과 모음으로 만들어요. 자음이 열 개 있어요: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ. 모음도 있어요: ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. 이 자음과 모음을 합치면 글자가 돼요. 예를 들어, ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한이에요. 처음에는 어려웠지만 이제 조금 읽을 수 있어요. 내일 더 연습할 거예요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Today I studied Hangul for the first time. Hangul is made of consonants and vowels. There are ten consonants: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ. There are also vowels: ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ. When you combine these consonants and vowels, you get a character. For example, ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한. At first it was difficult, but now I can read a little. I will practice more tomorrow.

comprehensionQuestions.question: How many basic consonants does Minjun list in the diary?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 열 개 (ten) — ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅇ, ㅈ, ㅎ

comprehensionQuestions.question: What example does the diary give for how a syllable block is made?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ = 한 — a consonant (ㅎ) + a vowel (ㅏ) + a final consonant (ㄴ) combine into one spoken syllable block

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 이에요/예요 copula forms in the text. Why does each one appear, and when does the ending change from 이에요 to 예요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 한이에요 (한 ends in consonant ㄴ → 이에요), 글자가 돼요 (not a copula, but a change-of-state verb 되다). The rule: 이에요 attaches after a final consonant (받침), 예요 attaches after a vowel. So 한글이에요 (ㄹ final) vs. 모음이에요 (ㅁ final) vs. 한이에요 (ㄴ final) — but if the word ended in a vowel, it would be 예요.

culturalNote.title: 한글날 — The Holiday That Celebrates an Alphabet
culturalNote.body: October 9th is 한글날 (Hangul Day), a national holiday in South Korea celebrating the promulgation of Hangul in 1443 by King Sejong the Great. This makes Korean one of the only languages in the world with a holiday dedicated to its writing system. King Sejong commissioned Hangul because the existing Chinese characters (한자) were so difficult that ordinary people could not read or write — only the elite could. He designed Hangul specifically to be learned quickly by everyone. Historical records say it could be learned 'in a morning' by a wise person and 'in ten days' by a less clever person. Modern linguists consider it one of the most scientifically designed writing systems ever created. When you struggle with a new letter, remember: King Sejong designed it so that you would not have to struggle for long.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which character is the vowel ㅏ (the sound 'a' as in 'father')?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅏ has a vertical stroke with a short tick pointing RIGHT. ㅓ looks similar but the tick points LEFT (that is the 'uh/eo' sound). ㅗ is a horizontal stroke with a tick pointing UP (the 'o' sound). ㅣ is just a vertical bar with no tick (the 'ee' sound). The direction of the tick is the key distinguishing feature.

inlineExercises.prompt: The syllable block 한 is made of which components?
inlineExercises.explanation: Korean syllable blocks follow the order: (1) initial consonant at top-left, (2) vowel to the right or below, (3) optional final consonant at the bottom. So 한 = ㅎ (initial) + ㅏ (vowel, to the right because it is a tall vowel) + ㄴ (final, at the bottom). The other options have the order wrong or use the wrong vowel — ㅓ would give 헌, not 한.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which of these is the SILENT consonant placeholder used when a syllable starts with a vowel sound?
inlineExercises.explanation: ㅇ in the onset (initial) position makes no sound — it is a placeholder that allows vowel-initial syllables to have a proper block shape. So 아 is written as ㅇ+ㅏ, not just ㅏ floating alone. ㅎ makes an 'h' sound, ㅅ makes an 's' sound, ㄴ makes an 'n' sound. Only ㅇ is silent at the start of a syllable (though it makes 'ng' at the end).

inlineExercises.prompt: How do you say 'Please speak slowly' in Korean?
inlineExercises.explanation: 천천히 = slowly, 말해 주세요 = please speak (V + 아/어 주세요 pattern). 다시 들어요 means 'listen again', 알겠어요 means 'I understand', 모르겠어요 means 'I don't know'. The V + 아/어 주세요 pattern (pattern-015) is used for polite requests for someone to perform an action for you.

inlineExercises.prompt: A student writes the romanization 'dasi duteeoyo' for 다시 들어요. What is wrong?
inlineExercises.explanation: 듣다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb: the final ㄷ of the stem changes to ㄹ before a vowel ending. So 듣 + 어요 → 들어요, NOT 듣어요. The pronunciation is 'deureoyo', not 'duteeoyo'. This is exactly why learning the actual Hangul matters — romanization based on the dictionary form 듣다 would mislead you. The written form 들어요 shows the actual pronunciation directly.

inlineExercises.prompt: Where does a TALL vowel like ㅏ, ㅓ, or ㅣ appear in a syllable block?
options: To the right of the consonant
inlineExercises.correct: To the right of the consonant
inlineExercises.explanation: Tall vowels (ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ, ㅐ, ㅔ and their compounds) sit to the RIGHT of the consonant: 가 (ㄱ+ㅏ), 서 (ㅅ+ㅓ), 시 (ㅅ+ㅣ). Wide vowels (ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ) sit BELOW the consonant: 고 (ㄱ+ㅗ), 수 (ㅅ+ㅜ). This layout rule is completely regular — once you know it, you can read any block.

inlineExercises.prompt: What does 알겠어요 most naturally mean in a classroom context?
inlineExercises.explanation: 알겠어요 literally contains 알다 (to know) + 겠 (future/inference marker) + 어요, but it functions as 'I got it / I understand / Okay' in conversation. It is NOT 모르겠어요 (I don't know / I'm not sure), NOT 다시 말해 주세요 (please say it again), NOT 맞아요? (is that right?). Use 알겠어요 to signal to your teacher that you have understood what they just explained.

bullets: Each Hangul syllable is a BLOCK built from: initial consonant + vowel (+ optional final consonant 받침) — read left-to-right, top-to-bottom within the block

MOUTH BLUEPRINTS: consonant shapes sketch the mouth position (ㅁ = closed lips, ㄴ = tongue at ridge, ㅇ = silent/circular). COMPASS ROSE: vowel ticks point in the direction of the mouth movement (ㅏ = right/open, ㅓ = left/back, ㅗ = up, ㅜ = down)
Romanization is a CHECKING TOOL, not Korean spelling — use it to verify your reading, then cover it and practice reading Hangul directly
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 2 introduces your first full sentences using 이다 (to be) and the topic marker 은/는 — you will use the Hangul you just learned to read and write complete Korean sentences like '저는 학생이에요' (I am a student).
